records.sourceFile: Estimating muscle fiber type composition in elite athletes - A survey on current practices and perceived merit.pdf

paper.citation: Lievens E, Van de Casteele F, De Block F, Van Vossel K, Vandenbogaerde T, Sandford GN, et al. Estimating Muscle Fiber-Type Composition in Elite Athletes: A Survey on Current Practices and Perceived Merit. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance. 2024 (ahead of print).
paper.abstract: This cross-sectional survey asked 446 high-performance coaches and sport-science or sports-medicine staff how they estimate athletes' muscle fiber-type composition and whether they consider it useful. Most experts relied on experience and jump tests rather than biopsy, and most used the information to individualize training volume and intensity. The authors conclude that some of the estimation methods in use lack scientific validity.
paper.tldr: Many high-performance staff use estimates of muscle fiber-type composition, mostly to individualize training volume and intensity. Most rely on experience, visual inspection and jump tests rather than biopsy, and some of these methods are not supported by validation evidence.
paper.methods: An online questionnaire in four languages was started by 740 people between February and April 2021; 32 athletes and 262 who answered only the first questions were excluded, leaving 446 experts (290 individual-sport, 104 team-sport, 52 both). Items covered demographics, use of MFTC and attitudes to biopsy, the general and sport-specific methods used to estimate MFTC, and the decisions MFTC informs. Differences between sport groups were tested with chi-square, ANOVA and related tests.
paper.findings: About 40% of experts used MFTC assessment for performance optimization, while 50% did not know their athletes' MFTC but would use it if they could assess it, and 10% saw no value in it. Experience or observation was the most common method (65%; 68% of individual-sport vs 51% of team-sport experts, P = .009), and jump tests were second (56%). Among current users, 87% used MFTC to individualize training volume and 84% to individualize training intensity. Fewer than 20% of experts thought their athletes would agree to a muscle biopsy.
paper.limitations: The paper has no separate limitations section. Its discussion notes that the sample was 88.6% male, that the share using biopsy and MRS (13.2% and 11.8%) suggests close academic involvement, that about 7% had no training in exercise physiology, and that results may not generalize to all coaches. Only 60% of people who started the survey were analyzed, and the athletes these experts serve ranged from world class (38.2%) to trained (17.7%).
paper.practicalImplications: Treat experience-based and visual estimates of fiber-type composition as unvalidated when planning athletes' training. The authors report that correlations between jump or strength tests and fiber type are often moderate, so most tests are not adequate estimators of fiber type.
paper.athleteDev: The survey shows that most high-performance users apply fiber-type estimates to individualize training volume and intensity. The paper does not show that these estimates improve training outcomes, so the decision should be tested in the athlete's own monitoring data before it changes the program.
paper.rtp: Not applicable to return to sport. The survey covers training and performance decisions and contains no injury, rehabilitation or return-to-play data.

records.sourceFile: Evaluating the Threshold Theory -      Can head impact indicators help.pdf

paper.citation: Mihalik JP, Lynall RC, Wasserman EB, Guskiewicz KM, Marshall SW. Evaluating the "Threshold Theory": Can Head Impact Indicators Help? Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2017;49(2):247-253.
paper.abstract: Analysis of 283,348 head impacts recorded by the Head Impact Telemetry System in 185 Division I football players over eight seasons, with 24 physician-diagnosed concussions. The authors tested how well linear acceleration thresholds from 50 g to 120 g predicted concussion.
paper.tldr: Head impact indicators based on linear acceleration thresholds flagged many impacts that did not cause concussion, so they should not be used alone to diagnose concussion. Positive predictive values were under 2% at every threshold tested.
paper.methods: Prospective data from one Division I program across eight seasons (2004 to 2012). Impacts were matched to physician-diagnosed concussions by time stamp and video review. The authors calculated sensitivity, specificity, positive and negative predictive value at each threshold, and repeated the analysis with concussion counts multiplied by five to allow for unreported cases.
paper.findings: Sensitivity fell from 95.8% at 50 g to 16.7% at 120 g, while specificity rose from 90.4% to 99.6%. Positive predictive value was at most 0.39% on the recorded data and no more than 1.94% after the fivefold adjustment; negative predictive value was 99.9% at all thresholds. In one season with 48 players, up to 2,092 evaluations would have been needed, with one diagnosed concussion.
paper.limitations: Only 24 concussions and one school, so sensitivity and predictive values are imprecise. Some unreported concussions may have been coded as noninjury. Many device thresholds are customizable or unpublished, and the study used HIT System data rather than the devices' own alerts.
paper.practicalImplications: Head impact indicators should not be used alone to diagnose concussion, because most alerts would trigger evaluations in uninjured athletes. Staff can still use sensor data to track repetitive head impacts and to find practices and games with high impact exposure.
paper.athleteDev: Impact sensors can show head-impact load and the practice and game situations that carry high exposure. They should not be used as a stand-alone measure of concussion or to replace the standard assessment.
paper.rtp: The study does not support using head impact thresholds to decide return to play or to clear an athlete after concussion. It evaluated concussion diagnosis, not return-to-sport decisions.

records.sourceFile: Evaluation of Minimum Reporting Limits to Determine In-Competition Use of Stimulants.pdf

paper.citation: Nair VS, Hanelli FA, Moore C, Goodrum JM, Miller GD, Crouch A, et al. Evaluation of Minimum Reporting Limits to Determine In-Competition Use of Stimulants. Drug Test Anal. 2025;17(6):915-922.
paper.abstract: Controlled administration of amphetamine, methylphenidate and modafinil to volunteers, with paired urine, serum, dried blood spot and oral fluid sampling, to test whether urinary minimum reporting limits can separate in-competition from out-of-competition use.
paper.tldr: A urinary reporting limit of 50 ng/mL cannot reliably separate in-competition from out-of-competition use of these stimulants. Serum and dried blood spots show systemic presence better, but still cannot separate the two periods.
paper.methods: Volunteers took one daily dose for five days, with urine, serum, dried blood spots and oral fluid collected during dosing and for 48 hours afterward. A single-dose group of two men was sampled to 96 hours. Analytes were measured by tandem mass spectrometry after validation for linearity, precision, accuracy and recovery.
paper.findings: In the multidose cohort, urinary concentrations of all target analytes were above 50 ng/mL at 48 hours after the last dose; methylphenidate parent was the exception and fell below the limit about 24 hours after the last dose. After a single dose, urinary amphetamine fell below 50 ng/mL by 72 hours, while modafinil acid stayed above it at 96 hours. Serum and dried blood spots showed detectable amounts at 48 hours in most volunteers, and oral fluid results were hard to interpret because they could not be normalized for hydration and viscosity.
paper.limitations: Volunteers were not athletes, and groups were small (4 to 6 per drug, two in the single-dose group). Dried blood spot results varied between spots in some samples, and oral fluid recovery was not estimated, so no matrix-specific cutoff could be set.
paper.practicalImplications: Anti-doping decisions should not assume that a urine positive for these stimulants reflects in-competition use, because urine stayed above the limit for two days after use. Athletes taking prescribed stimulants near competition need a valid therapeutic use exemption, and the authors suggest reviewing whether these drugs need a different reporting limit or status.
paper.athleteDev: Athletes taking prescribed stimulants can test positive days after their last dose, so a valid therapeutic use exemption matters. The study does not measure performance effects of these doses.
paper.rtp: Not applicable. The study concerns anti-doping detection in volunteers and does not address injury, rehabilitation or return to sport.

records.sourceFile: Evidence of ostarine cross-contamination via sweat in 2 athletes sharing the same neoprene hamstring sleeves.pdf

paper.citation: Kintz P, Gheddar L. Evidence of ostarine cross-contamination via sweat in 2 athletes sharing the same neoprene hamstring sleeves. An original situation of drug transfer where the anti-doping rule violation was suspended by the sport authorities. Clin Chim Acta. 2024;559:119688.
paper.abstract: Case report of ostarine transfer from one athlete's neoprene hamstring sleeves to a second athlete, supported by hair, nail and sleeve analysis by tandem mass spectrometry.
paper.tldr: Shared neoprene sleeves were a plausible route for ostarine to reach an athlete's urine. Hair and nail testing were key to the defense, but this single case does not show how common such transfer is.
paper.methods: Case analysis. Ostarine was measured in head hair, fingernail and toenail clippings from both athletes, and in 12 pieces (six per sleeve) of the two hamstring sleeves, using ultra-performance liquid chromatography with tandem mass spectrometry. The authors combined these results with the sport authority's investigation.
paper.findings: Athlete A had urine findings of 0.035 to 0.086 ng/mL, with ostarine not detected in hair or fingernails. Athlete B had ostarine at 190 pg/mg in hair, 780 pg/mg in fingernails and 45 pg/mg in toenails. Ostarine was found in all sleeve samples at 3 to 142 pg/g, and the sport authority accepted drug transfer and gave athlete A no fault or negligence.
paper.limitations: A single case with no controlled exposure, and the no-fault outcome is an authority decision reported by the authors, who also acted for the athlete's defense testing. The role of the medicinal skin cream in transfer is inferred, not measured.
paper.practicalImplications: This case suggests athletes should not share sweat-soaked skin-contact accessories such as sleeves, because a banned substance on them may reach the body through the skin. When an athlete faces a positive test with a very low urine concentration, hair and nail testing can help show whether long-term use is likely.
paper.athleteDev: Shared or sweat-soaked equipment can carry a banned substance and create an anti-doping risk. Athletes should not share sleeves or other skin-contact gear.
paper.rtp: Not applicable. The case concerns contamination and anti-doping rules, not injury care or rehabilitation.
